"Coder" is not the same as "software engineer".
A typical task in a real project usually involves different parts and integrations. It is not about writing an isolated piece of code. The main work is to understand what and where we should do. It is about knowing the context and making decisions. And the coding itself is only the last step (not really the last, because there is also testing the result and making fixes).

So if they can create a model that will act in an agent-like way and can get and keep context about a complex project (including participation in correspondence, team meetings, etc.) and use tools like IDEs to debug the result and deploy it to test environments - then we can call it "superhuman". Otherwise, it is just a good development tool - for a human.

comments.author: @atakanserin5260
comments.text:
I am a backend developer, it is true that AI makes things easy. There are some caveats I would like to share though:

- In order to operate with AI you need to know programming, and you need to be technical in your prompts. You basically need to program with it on much higher level but still you should know exactly what input and output you are aiming for. If you clear  on the "how" as well "what(input output)" the better it will perform. To know about the "how" you need to be an engineer.
- The smaller you make the tasks for AI the better it will perform, since you will clear out most of the details , naturally you will have a clearer communication with AI. But sometimes you get so small that you rather write the code yourself rather than prompt ping ponging. 
- You can not plug in and play AI written code. As a software engineer you need to own your code and know by heart what it is doing. Copy paste coding from AI is sophisticated way of doing cargo culting. You still need to go through in detail what it does.
- When you detect an error in AI generated code, usually I go with fixing it with prompting. But it sometimes turns round and round giving me wrong code. There I feel sort of a regret because I need to adapt to the AI written code and solution. Things would have been much easier if I just started from scratch.
- Because people use AI, Google search is not as good as before since it gets less hits and Google engineers just dumbed it down in order to cut the costs. Good thing with Google is(was) that it enabled you to find authentic solutions to authentic problems. On the other hand AI works more like returgitating what exists on the internet in a probabilistic manner. When you are stuck with a weird problem, AI is not really helpful because of its returgitative nature. Well Google is not helpful either since it is dumbed down. Furthermore as engineers we got worse Googling things since we are used to AI. Things sort of got harder on the authentic problem space according to my last 3 years of experience of AI-era. Weird problems took most of the time anyways even pre-AI era. AI's existence and its indirect effects on Google made the authentic/weird problem space harder to work with.
- Our job was to copy paste boilerplate code in most cases and fix it in the pre-AI era. AI did not change this workflow drastically.
- AI does not have big enough context/understanding to fit in a working code inside an XL production codebase that is divided among different components. It still does not have the nuanced thinking orchestrating different components together. Which sort of surprises me tbh.
- AI does not have dynamicity to capture weekly/daily changing documentation + architecture diagrams + slack notifications
- AI is not give aitohorization to act in the web or in an OS. Chatgpt interacts with APIs, Copilot can chage code and get it reviewed DevinAI is given sometype of authorization. But still there are alot of tools to be orchestrated to be acted on and fetch information from. AI is not here yet.
- Politically board members and such are playing for AI since they want to push the hope that AI will make some people obsolete and they would like to be the agent of change. Truth be told AI is great. But board members are putting a lot of money on marketing AI anxiety. Engineers are in big despair that they will be obsolete like this year or in near future. Some actually think they are obsolete now now. This phenomena naturally dips the market value of sw engineering. But as I discussed above, workflow of a software engineer is not changed drastically. Problems are still there and not solved by AI. You have to get your hands dirty and they get resolved more or less in the same amount of time, maybe a tiny bit less with AI and sometimes tiny bit more with AI. This value dip will lead engineers to give up or new candiates to not pick engineering. When this illusion of "we are obsolete" lifts off, I am curious to see what happens then.

At around 5:20, where Sam says that everyone can be like the head of the best company on the planet, and everyone can go do whatever they want; that is the problem.

All systems have constraints required to give them the form that they have.

Most people have vastly overly simplistic models of what those constraints actually are, particularly in respect of the natural world, but also in respect of the social world, and the financial, technological and cultural systems that allow people to survive in the natural world.      Very few appreciate how rapidly we are changing the relationships with the rest of the "natural world" and the levels of existential risk embodied within that.

Sam did not mention the word "responsibility".

The greater the level of freedom anyone claims, the greater the responsibility demanded if they (or the rest of us) are to survive the process.     It is great to learn to fly a plane, but it is not great if you end up crashing into some public space with it and killing dozens of people.

Freedom without appropriate levels of responsibility has to end badly - always, no escape.

Responsibility has to be part of this conversation, all levels, all domains - front and center, or the human experiment is about to end!!!

That may not be what Sam's ROI plans require, but it is what survival demands!

Freedom is an essential aspect of being human, it is a fundamental part of being able to search, of being creative, but responsibility has to be there too, it is part of what is demanded for survival.    There is an eternal and fundamentally uncertain tension between those two, and it gets more complex at each new level.    Unless Sam and the rest of the AI community start acknowledging and stressing that - we are all in deep trouble.    And if we do stress that, then the future can be better than most imagine possible.

I am all for the development of AI, but it has to be done responsibly, all levels, all domains, or the result will be as bad as many fear.

I remember the saying "A team is only as strong as its weakest link".
This always held very true from my university projects to real-life work where you often had to do overtime and do it "yourself" if you wanted it to be done perfect.
AI allows us to eliminate these "weakest links", enabling the best to do more themselves.
However, in the hands of the incompetent, AI will probably not help them in creating useful features/products either.

AI becoming a superhuman coder is impressive if true, but it will still be a tool that only people that already know what they are doing can use effectively.
Being a software developer or engineer is for more than just being a coder. It is about having vision and making good decisions. It is about having intuition.
That is something that still will hold value even when a lot of the Coding part can be replaced by AI soon.
Even the most amazing tool can only be as competent as its' wielder - a better developer will be able to achieve better results with AI than a worse one.

At least in the near future, I don't believe that we will see a significant decrease in demand for competent software developers.

However, I do believe that we will have a lot of problems in the future.
